t: Aim and plan of the session
n: This laboratory session is devoted to gas-liquid chromatography. The plan has two parts: first, becoming familiar with how gas-liquid chromatographs operate; second, qualitative determination of alcohols in blood and urine by the GLC method. That is, the aim is for students to learn how the chromatograph operates and to be able to determine alcohols in blood and urine qualitatively by GLC.

Three outcomes are expected from the session. First, the student becomes familiar with the operation of gas-liquid chromatographs. Second, the student learns to determine alcohols in blood and urine by GLC. Third, the student learns to distinguish the curves on the chromatogram, calculate retention time and measure curve height. These three skills form the basis of the whole work.

The following are needed for the work: distillate, flasks, test tubes, reagents, demonstration materials, adhesive tape and paper. The session takes place in a room equipped with special laboratory facilities. For the samples, a penicillin vial, that is, a flask, a rubber stopper, a fixator, 1 ml and 5 ml syringes and a stopwatch are used. Before starting work, check that all of this equipment is ready.

Gas chromatography is widely used to separate chemical substances and to determine their quality and quantity. The method is divided into two groups: gas-adsorption and gas-liquid chromatography. In gas-adsorption chromatography the stationary phase is a porous solid. In gas-liquid chromatography the stationary phase is a liquid coated on a porous solid. Remember: in both methods the mobile phase is a gas.

We distinguish the types of gas chromatography by the stationary phase. When the mobile phase is a gas and the stationary phase is a solid sorbent such as activated carbon, silica gel or aluminium oxide, this is gas-adsorption chromatography. If the stationary phase is a high-boiling liquid, this is gas-liquid chromatography, that is, GLC. In addition, gas chromatography is divided into separating (that is, elution), frontal and displacement methods.

Now let us look briefly at the history of chromatography. Chromatography was first used in 1903 by M. S. Tsvet to separate a complex mixture obtained from green plants. In 1941 Martin and Synge proposed paper chromatography and received the Nobel Prize; they also pointed to gas as a mobile phase. In 1952 James and Martin developed the methods of gas-adsorption and gas-liquid chromatography.

Let us consider how substances are separated in the column. A mixture of the substances under test is injected into a heated gas stream; the liquid mixture passes into the gaseous state in the thermostat at high temperature. In the column the substances undergo repeated adsorption and desorption between the stationary and gas phases and are separated. This means that the efficiency of separation depends on the distribution coefficient of the substances.

A gas chromatograph consists of the following parts: gas source, reducer, injector, column, thermostat, detector and a recording device. The gas, that is, nitrogen or argon, having passed through the reducer, is fed into the column together with the mixture. The quantity of gas is measured with a rheometer. The column is placed in the thermostat, and substances leaving the column pass to the detector and the recording device.

About the chromatographic column. The mixture is separated in columns in the form of a U-shaped, spiral or circular tube with a diameter of 2 mm to 12-15 mm and a length of 2 m to 20 m. Columns are made mainly of glass, copper, brass or steel. For the qualitative analysis of alcohols, the column size is 100 x 0.6 cm. Remember this size, because it is precisely this column that is used in practical work.

The separation of substances depends on several factors. It depends on the column being packed with sorbent at uniform density, on the nature of the sorbent, on the gas velocity and on the constancy of the column temperature. The main inert gases are nitrogen, helium and argon. Silica gel, aluminium oxide, activated carbon and also synthetic porous substances, that is, chemosorb and polysorb, are used as sorbents.

The detector is one of the main parts of a gas chromatograph: a change in the composition of the gas leaving the column shows itself precisely in the detector. Detectors are divided into integral and differential types. The signal of an integral detector is directly proportional to the total mass of substance in the gas stream. In pure gas it gives a horizontal line, and in a mixture a stepped line forms. A differential detector, by contrast, shows the change in quantity with time.

A differential detector shows the change in the quantity of substance per unit time; most detectors are of this kind. Differential detectors are divided into concentration and flow types. An example of a concentration detector is the katharometer, which is based on the change in thermal conductivity. An example of a flow detector is the flame ionisation detector, which is based on the electrical conductivity of the flame.

t: Katharometer: why it is used in alcohol analysis
n: Let us consider why a katharometer is used in alcohol analysis. In the analysis of most volatile drugs, a detector based on the change in thermal conductivity of gases, that is, the katharometer, is used. The katharometer is universal for the detection of many substances. Its sensitivity is lower than that of the flame ionisation and other detectors, 10-2 - 10-3, but it is simple and convenient. Among detectors, electron capture detectors are the most sensitive.

According to structure and mode of operation, detectors are divided into four types: the katharometer, flame ionisation, electron capture, and the thermionic detector. The katharometer is based on the difference in thermal conductivity; it is a concentration detector and is universal. The flame ionisation detector is a flow detector based on a hydrogen flame and electrical conductivity. Among detectors, electron capture detectors are the most sensitive. In general, detectors are integral or differential.

Detector pulses are measured with sensitive potentiometers and recorded on chromatographic paper. The curve on the paper is called a chromatogram, and each curve is characteristic of an individual substance separated in the column. A chromatogram is characterised by retention time, that is, distance, height, base and area. As the table shows, retention time is a qualitative indicator and area is a quantitative one.

t: Retention time is a qualitative indicator
n: Retention time, that is, retention distance, is the time that passes from the injection of the substance into the column until it leaves the column in the greatest quantity. When the analysis conditions are kept constant, retention time is the parameter that determines the identity of substances. In the analysis of blood and urine, the emergence time of the curves is compared with the time obtained for the standard solutions. Thus, if the times match, the substance is considered identified.

Let us see what true retention time is. Retention time is the time or distance from injection of the substance into the column until the maximum peak is formed. The retention time of a gas not sorbed by the sorbent is called the dead retention time. The true retention time of a substance equals the retention time of the substance-gas mixture minus the dead retention time. In the formula: t true equals t total minus t m. The same applies for distance: l true equals l total minus l m.

t: Methods of qualitative analysis in GLC
n: Qualitative analysis is carried out by retention parameters in the chromatographic column, that is, by time or distance. For this, comparison is made with a standard substance or a mixture of them. In addition, chemical reactions are carried out before and after chromatography. GLC can also be combined with physical methods such as UV, IR, mass spectrometry, luminescence and NMR.

We begin with preparation for the analysis. Each student receives from the instructor a solution prepared from a mixture of different alcohols and begins to analyse it by GLC. Before work, make sure that the stoppers in the injector block are tightly closed: soap solution is applied to the point where the syringe needle is inserted. If no soap bubbles appear, the injector block is tightly closed. If bubbles form, the rubber stopper is replaced in the presence of the instructor. The tightness of the stoppers is checked throughout the whole session.

The next step is checking the microsyringe. Each student carries out the check with 1 µl syringes. 0.5 µl of acetone is drawn into the syringe and dropped onto filter paper: a microdrop should form at the tip of the needle. When touched to the paper, it leaves a small damp spot. If no microdrop forms, the microsyringe is recalibrated by turning the screw that holds the needle.

The procedure for checking chromatograph sensitivity and air. When checking sensitivity, when the pen on the air curve reaches half the height of the maximum, the sensitivity level is rapidly switched to the "100" position. In doing so, the height of the water curve decreases. The chromatographic analysis of water vapour and air is checked at the beginning, middle and end of the laboratory session. If a doubtful result is obtained, the check is performed together with the instructor.

The first part of the conditions for alcohol analysis. Chromatographic column size 100 x 0.6 cm. Solid-phase particles 0.25-0.5 mm; this is INZIM-600 brick treated with alkali and alkyl sulphate salts, 0.3 g each. The stationary phase is Shostakovsky balsam, that is, vinylin, impregnated at a ratio of 1:5 to the solid phase.

The second part of the analysis conditions is the operating parameters. The mobile phase, that is, the gas, is nitrogen, at a nitrogen flow rate of 50-60 ml/min. The temperature of the column and detector is 75 °C. The chromatograph recording scale is 1:1, detector current 60-100 mA, paper tape speed 720 mm/h. The time of injection of the mixture and the recording times of the highest points of the curves are noted.

Now, preparing alkyl nitrites from alcohols. The tape is started: first an air sample is injected, then the mixture of alkyl nitrites. 0.5 ml of the alcohol mixture, 0.5 ml of 50% trichloroacetic acid and 0.25 ml of 30% sodium nitrite are placed in the vessel and mixed for 1 minute, and then 2 ml of the gas-air portion is injected into the injector. The vessel is closed with a rubber stopper and placed in a special sealing device. The book sets the task of writing the equation of the reaction with sodium nitrite.

The procedure for recording standard results. The time of injection of the mixture and the recording times, or distances, of the highest points of the chromatogram curves are noted. Everything is entered in the student's laboratory notebook. The examination of alkyl nitrites is repeated three times and entered in special tables.

t: Determining ethyl alcohol in blood and urine: tasks
n: There are four tasks in determining ethyl alcohol in blood and urine. The first is working on gas chromatographs equipped with a katharometer detector. The second is drawing up an accurate calibration table with the selected internal standards. The third is converting the alcohols in blood and urine into alkyl nitrites. The fourth is taking an accurate sample from the vapour-gas phase and injecting it into the injector block of the chromatograph.

t: Preparing a blood or urine sample
n: Preparing a blood or urine sample. Into a penicillin vial, 0.5 ml of 50% trichloroacetic acid solution is placed, and 0.5 ml of blood or urine on top. The vial is closed with a rubber stopper and placed in the fixator; the fixator is needed to hold the rubber stopper. After mixing, 0.25 ml of 30% sodium nitrite is injected with a 1 ml syringe and the vial is shaken for 1 minute.

Converting alcohols to alkyl nitrites. The qualitative and quantitative determination of alcohols in blood and urine is based on converting them into alkyl nitrites and separating them chromatographically. Alkyl nitrites are several times more volatile than the corresponding alcohols. Trichloroacetic acid is placed in the vial, then blood or urine, sodium nitrite solution is added with a syringe, and then a sample is taken from the vapour-gas phase. The reaction proceeds in the closed vial with shaking for 1 minute.

t: Injecting the sample into the chromatograph
n: Injecting the sample into the chromatograph. With a 5 ml syringe, 3 ml is taken from the air-gas portion inside the vial and rapidly injected into the injector block. The stopwatch is started at the moment of injecting the air-gas mixture, and the recording of the chromatogram is observed. The time to the height of each curve emerging on the chromatogram is noted.

Comparing and interpreting the result. The times noted are compared with the times obtained from the standard solutions. The student must be able to distinguish the curves, calculate retention time and measure curve height. The height of the curve depends on the quantity of alcohols; the difference is assessed on this basis.

t: Methods of quantitative analysis in GLC
n: In gas chromatographic analyses, the quantity of a substance is determined in three ways: internal standard, absolute calibration and internal normalisation. The quantity of alcohol is determined by the internal standard method, and propyl alcohol is taken as the internal standard. The calculation is made from a calibration graph.

Calculation with an internal standard. Propyl alcohol is taken as the internal standard, and the calculation is made from a calibration graph. The graph is constructed from the ratio of the height of the ethyl nitrite peak h1 to the height of the propyl nitrite peak h2, and the concentration of the substance. The unknown sample is found from the graph on the basis of this ratio of h1 to h2. An accurate calibration table is drawn up with the selected internal standards.

Let us list the advantages and the disadvantage of GLC. GLC is a universal method; it separates complex mixtures into components; the analysis takes little time and little substance. The method has sufficient sensitivity and high accuracy: the relative error is about ±1.0-1.5%. As a disadvantage, the volatility and instability of some liquid stationary phases is mentioned.

Safety and working procedure. The tightness of the stoppers in the injector block is checked throughout the session. If bubbles appear, the rubber stopper is replaced in the presence of the instructor. If a doubtful result is obtained, the check is performed together with the instructor. For the laboratory work the student brings rubber gloves, a wipe and a face mask; this is the requirement of the introductory session.

t: Parts of the apparatus and their functions (1)
n: Parts of the apparatus and their functions, first part. As a quick quiz, the task is to match the name and function of a numbered part in the diagram. The cylinder is intended to supply the mobile phase to the chromatograph. The flow stabiliser delivers the gas flow evenly. The injector is the device for introducing the sample, and in the chromatographic column the substances are separated.

t: Parts of the apparatus and their functions (2)
n: Parts of the apparatus and their functions, second part. The self-recording device records the results of the analysis. The detector converts the change in the properties of the gas flow into an electrical signal. The columns are placed and heated in the thermostat. The manometer measures the gas pressure in the column, and the flow meter measures the quantity of gas leaving.

A practical situation, that is, case 7. First-year students prepared a weak drink smelling of pear for a celebration; in those who drank it, nausea, abdominal pain, dizziness and weakness appeared after 1 hour. After half an hour, effects on the CNS were observed: drowsiness, stupor, dilated pupils, a fall in blood pressure. Preliminary information: the breath of the poisoned persons smelled of fusel oil. Aim: to isolate the volatile poison and show the procedure of analysis.

The solution pathway for case 7. In the case, those who drank the weak alcoholic drink with a pleasant pear smell prepared by first-year students had nausea, abdominal pain, dizziness and weakness. Amyl and isoamyl alcohols are often present in samogon and act on the central nervous system. Therefore the smell of fusel oil raises the probability of amyl alcohols. Then follow steam distillation, extraction of the distillate with ether, conversion to alkyl nitrites with comparison of retention time against the standard, confirmation by the violet-red colour with salicylaldehyde, and determination of the quantity by the internal standard method, that is, propyl alcohol.
